**1. Can the Galaxy Note be a Game Changer?** 
**1) Is the size burdensome?** 
In fact, just yesterday I saw a woman in Bundang making a call with a Galaxy Tab, and I've seen many seniors show interest in large, tablet-sized phones. Furthermore, a larger screen size for wider web browsing, HD-quality videos, and work is a welcome feature for many. An HD-quality screen on a 4-inch device is highly likely to cause eye fatigue. When I used early smartphones like the Cellvic XG, MyCube, and Poz series, many friends asked why I used such a ridiculously large smartphone. Eventually, the iPhone came out and shattered people's preconceptions about large touchscreens. I believe the Note's large screen size is also a manageable size if it offers users convenience beyond that. In fact, the reactions from other 5-inch device users haven't been bad either.


**2) The amazing S Pen, Wacom hurray!** 
While those who haven't used it disparage the S Pen, the S Pen's technology is Wacom's technology. It's one of the technologies I consider the ultimate interface. Electromagnetic resonance (EMR) pen technology supports precise pressure and tilt detection, allowing it to perfectly mimic the effects of a real brush or pencil, making it favored by graphic designers. In fact, people who draw game illustrations, webtoons, etc., which you see, each have a tablet with this technology. Therefore, I won't discuss the completeness of this technology separately. If I were to compare the S Pen to a capacitive stylus, I would dare say it's like comparing a professional drawing pen to a twig. If the iPhone's designer sketched digitally, they would have certainly used a Wacom tablet. 
Some people say that capacitive touch and the Wacom pen cannot be used simultaneously, but there are already laptops like the TM2 that use both capacitive touch and a Wacom pen. The EMR pen activates when it comes within a certain distance of the screen, at which point capacitive touch is deactivated. 
This Wacom technology is quite old, and many companies covet it, but apparently, no one can use this technology except Wacom. That's why even Microsoft invested in an alternative technology called N-trig, but it can't match Wacom's performance. 
Of course, this technology is not Samsung's. And the S Pen is not on the same level as an Intuos, which graphic designers use and supports tilt detection. Still, with 128 levels of pressure sensitivity, it's slightly lower than the ArtPad 2 I used way back in the 20th century, but it's more than capable of creating excellent images.
For reference, the images in the [Illustration] category of my blog are drawings made using a Wacom tablet, similar to the S Pen.

**3) What happens when HD meets the pen? What changes?**
**- PC web screen can be used as is**
The true meaning of a larger screen and precise pen input lies in the ability to browse PC-optimized websites without any inconvenience. Currently, most PC web services are designed based on a mouse interface. Wacom's S Pen can do everything a mouse can, from mouse-over effects to clicking small menu items. Even if current Galaxy or iPhone devices could full-browse PC web pages, the reason they had to pinch-zoom and then touch certain areas was precisely because finger touch couldn't replace the precision of a mouse. However, the pen makes that possible. Selecting all content without zooming. While this goes against recent considerations for touch-based web design, for immediate users, since most websites are not optimized for touch, the benefits that can be enjoyed are very significant.
**- Development of new UX**
The combination of pen and touch announced by Microsoft can be realized. Of course, the Galaxy Note has an either-or structure for touch and pen, so Microsoft's new patent cannot be applied. However, the fact that Samsung and Microsoft have signed a cross-licensing agreement for patents means that Microsoft's patents could be applied to Samsung's tablets in the future, and entirely new UX could emerge. If there are people who claim that the pen won't bring any changes, I'd like to tell them to remember what changes the Nintendo DS Lite brought.
 
 
**[ Microsoft's touch and pen-based UX planned for Windows 8 ]****
**
**2. However, LTE tackled the Note's side**
**- Users want 3G!** 
Another topic of this post, which has been praising the Galaxy Note, is LTE. It seems Samsung has created a wonderful device that could wash away the stigma of copying the iPhone, but in Korea, there's someone who strongly tackled it: LTE. Following my criticism of the KT Galaxy Tab 8.9, I'd like to tell another story of the Note being ruined by a carrier's strategy.

**1) LTE for top specifications?**
They say LTE was chosen for the Note because it's for top specifications. However, what about sacrificing the CPU for LTE? In Korea, for LTE, they abandoned Exynos and adopted the inferior Snapdragon. For the higher HD-level resolution, a high-performance CPU and GPU are very significant. In fact, the need is greater for the Note than for the Galaxy S2. Nevertheless, Samsung sacrificed performance for the sake of LTE network speed. The statement that LTE was chosen for top specifications doesn't quite add up.

**2) Do consumers want LTE?**
That's a ridiculous claim. They might keep running ads to inject it into the public. In fact, they already are. But it's a reality that those in the know are aware of. Let me show you a few amusing results I've seen recently.
 

**- Galaxy Note Recommended Search Terms Results**
**{{IMG:1}} **
 
Two of the recommended search terms are related to 3G. LTE isn't even there.

**- Search results for Galaxy Note on Junggonara (Used Market)**
**{{IMG:2}}

******
**Currently, 3G models are being sold with a premium. ㅡㅡ;** **Do people really want LTE?**

**3) Does Samsung not know consumer needs or have no intention to do business?**
Samsung is not a group of such foolish people, and many bloggers who reviewed the Galaxy Note also pointed this out. They are well aware of consumer needs, even mentioning 3G at events.

**3) Pressure from carriers to make it a strategic phone for LTE**
The conclusion is one: there must have been a deal or some kind of pressure from the carriers. It's incredibly frustrating. Clearly, buying a domestic model is more convenient than importing a Note through unofficial channels from overseas, so a certain level of purchase will definitely occur. However, while precise measurement may be difficult, it's clear that LTE held the Note back. If this model had been released with 3G, the carriers would have been afraid of the Note consuming more traffic and using unlimited data plans.

**4. While carriers raise communication fees and strengthen control over service and device markets, the government stands idly by**
Even if the current 62,000 won plan had been set at around 55,000 won, I wouldn't have been this annoyed. The 62,000 won plan is also not unlimited, but it allows a level of traffic that most 55,000 won plan users would find acceptable. The government, which claims to lower communication fees, is only lowering them in irrelevant areas. Data communication fees are now as essential as electricity. Perhaps those in power only consider voice calls as essential. The wisdom of past governments, which worried about the problems brought by the digital divide, seems to be only concerned with digital control now. Data communication fees are essential, and I hope the government doesn't stand idly by in this situation where they are increasing by more than 10% at once. 
And this money is directly felt by users as an increase in phone prices, becoming a reason not to choose Samsung phones, so Samsung Electronics should also reconsider. Isn't this the reason why the Note, which is already more expensive than the Galaxy S2, feels even more expensive?
